The dose (10 mg IM) is the standard approved dose for acute agitation, so binding is pharmacologically expected, but it was not directly measured here. Per the round-28 AFFECTS rule, no affects record is emitted since engagement was not demonstrated or implied by PD data.

2. PATHWAY MODULATION: No pathway biomarkers were reported. We cannot assess whether D2 receptor antagonism translated to downstream sedation/agitation-reduction biology from the data provided.

3. CLINICAL TRANSLATION: The primary endpoint (PANSS-EC change from baseline at 2 hours) was clearly missed: olanzapine -4.7 vs placebo -4.6, difference ~-0.1, p=0.94. This is a near-perfect null result. Across all time points (15, 30, 60, 90 min), the placebo arm tracked almost identically to the active arm, with p-values ranging from 0.62 to 1.0. The responder analysis (≥40% PANSS-EC decrease at 2 hours) showed 3 olanzapine vs 4 placebo responders. ACES sedation scores were also identical between arms at all time points.

4. POPULATION EFFECTS: No differential subgroup responses were identified. The placebo response was remarkably high and nearly identical to the active treatment at every time point, suggesting a dominant high placebo response rather than a subgroup-specific effect.

5. CONFOUNDERS: The most striking feature of this trial is the extremely high and nearly identical placebo response. Both arms showed substantial PANSS-EC reductions (~4.6-4.7 points at 2 hours), suggesting that the act of receiving an injection, being in a clinical setting, or natural resolution of the agitation episode drove most of the observed improvement. The sample size is very small (N=34 total), making the trial severely underpowered to detect a treatment difference even if one existed. The combination of high placebo response and small N is the dominant failure pattern here. Olanzapine IM is an established, approved treatment for acute agitation in schizophrenia, so the failure here is most parsimoniously explained by high placebo response masking a real drug effect in a very small sample, rather than a true mechanistic failure.

The near-identical means and high p-values (0.62-1.0 across all time points) are consistent with insufficient statistical power to detect a real treatment effect even if one exists.

review_reason: The near-perfect null result (p=0.94, difference of -0.1 PANSS-EC units) in a very small sample (N=34) with an established, approved drug (olanzapine IM) raises the question of whether this was a failed trial of a known-effective drug due to high placebo response and severe underpowering, rather than a true mechanistic failure. Expert review is warranted to assess: (1) whether the placebo response rate in this trial was unusually high compared to historical benchmarks for acute agitation in schizophrenia; (2) whether the sample size was adequate for the expected effect size based on prior olanzapine IM trials; and (3) whether the trial setting or patient selection may have contributed to the high placebo response (e.g., less severely agitated patients, different clinical context).
